summary: After a 27 June 2026 domestic disturbance in Spokane, police issued a July 1 release that first said a dachshund had died and then corrected the dog’s condition to serious injury. Seeking a photo to accompany the correction, police personnel sent news media an image apparently showing a real undercover officer holding the dog with a cast. Police asked media not to publish the officer’s identity. The Spokesman-Review cropped out identifying features and published the dog image. Police then disclosed that detectives had generated the scene as a joke; a supervisor had mistaken it for a real photograph and passed it through a communications handoff. The local paper reported the image’s synthetic origin after learning it. The animal injury and arrest were real reported events; the photograph’s dog scene was fabricated. The generation file, internal message chain and exact reach of the initial image are not public.

assessment_boundaries: The police release establishes the real injury and initial dog-status correction, but it does not itself authenticate or discuss the later synthetic photograph.

vigil_assessment.factual_basis: The official Spokane police release directly records the underlying June 27 domestic disturbance and a July 1 correction that the dog survived with serious injury. The Spokesman-Review’s July 20 account says police supplied an image of a real undercover officer in a fabricated dog scene; the newsroom cropped and published the dog portion, after which it learned the image was AI generated. The newspaper attributes to police public information officer Tricia Leming the explanation that detectives created it as a joke, a supervisor believed it real, and a separate communications official requested an incident image that the supervisor passed along. That is first-party police explanation carried by local reporting, not direct review of internal messages or image metadata. AIID aggregates only the same underlying report. The later city clocktower flyer involved a different department and is recorded separately as INC-000079. In the same local report, police information officer Leming called the transfer a genuine mistake and said SPD was reviewing and strengthening its image-verification processes. This is a reported prospective response, not evidence that a required verification control previously existed or had failed to activate. The originating newsroom places the request to suppress the officer’s identity before its crop and publication. That request concerned identity exposure; it did not disclose the synthetic scene.
vigil_assessment.governance_interpretation: A synthetic joke image acquired official evidentiary weight when its origin and context were lost in police handoffs. The newsroom then relied on the apparent authenticity of the police-supplied image, though it cropped the undercover officer. The real dog injury and the separate police correction remain distinct from this provenance failure. Police attributed the image to their own incident communications, which was a real supplying institution; the material error was loss of its synthetic creation state and non-evidentiary context, rather than a proven false attribution to a named creator. The synthetic state and joke context failed to persist through official handoff; source institution attribution and the genuine dog injury remain distinct. The officer crop is not automatically a C2PA assertion redaction. Independent external assessment finds the usable origin-tracing outcome Not aligned. Materially relevant transparency-history and lineage-practice requirements remain Boundary where decisive process evidence is unavailable. Absent C2PA operations and different model-training/interaction objects are audit-only; the real-dog correction is not evidence of successful synthetic-image repair.
vigil_assessment.significance_to_cam: This case shows how an image can move from informal internal creation to an official public artefact without a provenance check. Source and transformation receipts at each handoff would have exposed the synthetic status before the newsroom used it.
